doc.title: Horn Shirley — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Growing up in Woodridge and whether race mattered
summary: She describes the working-class Woodridge neighborhood and her family nearby; she recalls no racial awareness, mentioning Aunt Cleo in St. Louis.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Okay. And did all of you all grow up in Brooklyn? Did your family reside in Brooklyn?
No, darling. We all resided right here in Washington, right here in this area is called . . .
Oh, Woodridge.
Woodridge, right.
Okay, so we were [unclear].
No, no, no, this is Woodridge here.
Can you describe the neighborhood at the time, both the racial composition as well as the socioeconomic composition, the school systems, etc., as you remember them as a child?
Well, you know, there was a difference here. There‘s ten years‘ difference between my brother, my oldest brother and me, you know. Ask that question again.
The neighborhood, just your recollections of the neighborhood when you were growing up, both the racial composition as well as the socioeconomic makeup of your neighborhood.

Oh, it was really always . . . it was kind of mellow, you know, always here, because my brothers always, you know, they were hoodlums. They‘re both hoodlums. However, the neighborhood was always nice.
Was it basically working-class people?

Yes, yes, right, right. I mean, my mom and dad and my brothers, they were here. I moved here like maybe twenty-four years ago, and before that I had my daughter, and we were in Dupont Park. My daughter was born, and of course I had to move over here close to my mom and my dad, and my aunt was there, and my uncles over there.
There‘s a natural support system.
Yes. Yes.
Now, just to be clear again, the neighborhood was segregated, or was it an interracial, I mean an integrated neighborhood?
You know, I don‘t really . . . I really don‘t know. You mean here?
When you were growing up; obviously not now. It‘s changed incredibly. But as a child, do you remember?

No, I don‘t, I really don‘t know, because my dad‘s from St. Louis, and I had my Aunt Cleo, you know, who taught Miles [Davis] and stuff, because Miles didn‘t . . . he didn‘t talk about black and white and all that other stuff. It was people. I remember him telling me my aunt was mean. She was a mean teacher. But I remember going into St. Louis and going to the school, and Aunt Cleo was rough. Ooh, she was mean. But I don‘t remember, because my dad was . . . I don‘t know. I don‘t know about black and white. It was like . . .
So it didn‘t really impact you.
No, not at all. I mean, we were just us.
